name: Polyphasic sleep
lead: Polyphasic sleep is the practice of dividing sleep into several separate periods across 24 hours, usually more than two, rather than one consolidated nighttime block. The term was used in the early twentieth century by psychologist J. S. Szymanski to describe animal activity patterns.[1] In online communities it refers to schedules, such as Uberman and Everyman, that aim to cut total sleep to a few hours using short naps.[1][2]

Historical research suggests segmented nighttime sleep was common in pre-industrial Europe, a view argued by historian A. Roger Ekirch in 2001, though a 2015 study of three pre-industrial societies found monophasic nighttime sleep and Ekirch has questioned its conclusions.[1] Wikipedia states there is no scientific evidence that extreme reduced-sleep schedules are effective or beneficial.[1] A 2021 National Sleep Foundation consensus panel report addressed the adverse impact of polyphasic sleep patterns in humans.[3]

paras: Everyman uses roughly three hours of core sleep plus three 20-minute naps; Uberman uses a nap about every four hours totalling about three hours; the Buckminster Fuller pattern used 30-minute naps every six hours.[1] Grokipedia also lists Dymaxion and biphasic variants.[2]

Ekirch documented references to a 'first sleep' and 'second sleep' separated by waking.[1] Buckminster Fuller reportedly kept intermittent sleeping for two years in the 1940s, a 1943 Time article said, and stopped because it conflicted with his associates' schedules.[1] Claudio Stampi studied polyphasic strategies in solo sailors.[1]

A 1992 study by Thomas Wehr found men kept in 14 hours of darkness daily settled into two sleep blocks with waking between.[1] A 1989 field study of 99 sailors concluded that polyphasic strategies improved sustained performance, though military and aviation reports note performance on ultrashort sleep stays below fully rested levels.[1] NASA-supported nap research by David Dinges found longer naps were generally better and nighttime naps could cause sleep inertia lasting up to an hour.[1] Sleep medicine bodies such as the Sleep Foundation say the schedules lack support for claimed productivity benefits and risk sleep deprivation, according to Grokipedia, which is AI-generated.[2] The NSF consensus panel report discusses adverse impacts.[3]
Chronic sleep restriction, circadian misalignment and microsleeps during waking hours have been described.[1][2] Involuntary polyphasic sleep also occurs in irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder.[1]

Small studies include Stampi's sailor work (1989), a 49-day single-subject experiment reportedly including all sleep stages, and a 2021 National Sleep Foundation consensus report on adverse effects.[1][3] No randomised trials show that extreme polyphasic schedules deliver benefits in healthy adults were located.

timeline.event: Time article reports Buckminster Fuller's intermittent sleeping.[1]
Ekirch publishes work on segmented pre-industrial sleep.[1]
NSF consensus panel report on polyphasic sleep.[3]

lore.intro: Wikipedia notes an online community that experiments with alternative schedules to increase waking productivity.[1]

claims.claim: Short naps can replace most nighttime sleep and free up hours.
claims.believers: Proponents say naps timed to capture REM sleep efficiently let the body adapt to a few hours of total sleep.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states there is no scientific evidence these schedules are effective; the NSF panel reported adverse impacts.[1][3]

claims.claim: Pre-industrial humans naturally slept in segments, so polyphasic sleep is natural.
claims.believers: Citing Ekirch's historical record of 'first' and 'second' sleep.[1]
claims.experts: Historical evidence for biphasic nights is debated; a 2015 study of three pre-industrial societies found monophasic sleep.[1]

card.summary: Splitting sleep into naps to sleep far less; historically interesting, and expert panels report adverse impacts.
card.note: Chronic sleep restriction risk; NSF panel reports adverse impact.

quick.overview:
Polyphasic sleep means sleeping in several short blocks per day instead of one long night. Online schedules like Uberman try to cut total sleep to two to four hours.

Biphasic or segmented sleep has a documented history, but evidence that extreme reduction works is absent, and a 2021 expert panel reported adverse effects.
quick.mechanism: Followers time short naps to catch REM or deep sleep early, relying on adaptation. Evidence for this is limited to small, short studies.
quick.risks: Sleep restriction, circadian disruption and microsleeps are the main risks reported by sleep organisations.
